entry.title: The Internet Has a Trust Problem

link.title: The Internet Has a Trust Problem

entry.content:
By Melisa K. Savich
Beyond Authentication · Article 1

A colleague messages you from the account you talk to every day. They need a sensitive file sent to a new address.

The name is familiar. The conversation history is there. The request sounds like them.

Do you send it?

You might first check whether it’s really your colleague. But suppose you could establish that it is. They might still be mistaken about who should receive the file—or asking you to bypass a rule.

This hypothetical request captures the question behind Beyond Authentication: what evidence do we need before deciding to act?

A successful identity check helps. It doesn’t finish the job.

A stronger login answers a specific question

Authentication helps establish that someone controls an authenticator associated with an account. Identity proofing is a separate process that connects an online subject to a real-life person, with a stated degree of assurance (Temoshok, Fenton, et al., 2025; Temoshok, Abruzzi, et al., 2025).

Neither tells us whether sending that file is a good idea.

Passkeys improve an important part of this picture. They use public-key credentials bound to the relevant service, helping resist phishing. That’s a real benefit, not a reason to declare authentication solved—or pointless (FIDO Alliance, n.d.).

But even a well-protected account can make an inappropriate request.

For our colleague’s message, three questions matter:

Question What it helps establish
Who is making the request? Evidence about identity and account control.
Are they entitled to ask? Whether the action fits their authority.
Should I comply here? Whether the destination, purpose, and consequences are acceptable.

This is a way to organize the decision, not a checklist that guarantees safety.

We can have a convincing answer to the first question while the other two remain wide open.

Familiarity is useful—and exploitable

Business email compromise shows why that distinction matters.

The FBI describes schemes involving spoofed addresses, compromised legitimate accounts, and access to genuine billing conversations. These are different mechanisms, but each can make a fraudulent request look familiar (Federal Bureau of Investigation [FBI], n.d., 2024).

An imitation account raises one problem: the sender isn’t who they claim to be. A compromised account raises another: the address may be genuine, but someone else is operating it.

Our opening example adds a third possibility. Your colleague really is asking, but the disclosure still isn’t appropriate. That’s a hypothetical policy failure, not an incident established by the FBI reports.

These distinctions change what would help. Strong authentication can help prevent takeover. Independent confirmation can help verify a changed destination. A narrower permission can limit what gets disclosed.

The reassuring word verified leaves something out unless we also know what was verified.

Trust is bigger than an identity check

In sociology, trust involves more than collecting facts about an individual.

Lewis and Weigert (1985) describe trust as a social phenomenon with cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions. Their account emphasizes relationships and shared expectations: trust helps people cooperate without calculating every possible future.

That perspective is useful here because ordinary relationships aren’t a series of fresh identity checks. We develop expectations about people, then rely on those expectations when deciding what to do.

I might trust someone to recommend a book without giving them access to my email. The difference isn’t a contradiction. Those decisions put different things at risk.

That’s the distinction I want security systems to make easier to see: trust someone to do what, under which circumstances?

History can help answer that. It doesn’t answer it permanently.

NIST already recognizes reasonable, risk-based assurance for returning users and addresses session management. Authentication isn’t oblivious to continuity (Temoshok, Fenton, et al., 2025).

Still, continuity of account access and confidence in someone’s next request aren’t interchangeable. Even perfect evidence that it’s the same operator cannot establish that every future action serves your interests.

This raises a question for later essays: could someone build credibility through ordinary interactions, then use it to influence which requests—or explanations—we accept?

That’s a research question here. Email-compromise evidence alone doesn’t establish how sustained manipulation changes beliefs.

A trust system connects evidence to action

I’m using trust system as a working term for the arrangements that help us decide what to rely on, for what purpose, and what we can do when something goes wrong.

It isn’t one product or a universal score. It can include software, procedures, and relationships.

Consider a hypothetical payment workflow. A protected account identifies the employee. Permissions limit who can initiate a transfer. Another person approves it. A known contact route helps confirm changed bank details.

Each part addresses a different uncertainty. Together, they make the decision less dependent on one person recognizing that something feels wrong.

Here’s the distinction in a simple sketch:

flowchart TD
    A["A request arrives"] --> B{"Identity evidence sufficient?"}
    B -->|Unclear| C["Verify independently"]
    B -->|Yes| D{"Authority and consequences acceptable?"}
    D -->|Unclear or no| E["Pause, seek approval, or narrow the action"]
    D -->|Yes| F["Act with relevant safeguards"]

An illustrative decision sketch, not a validated algorithm. The second question still matters after the first is answered.

Do we actually need another layer?

Security practitioners could reasonably object that authentication and authorization are already separate concepts. Why dress that distinction up as an internet-wide trust problem?

It’s a fair challenge.

My argument isn’t that every system needs a new component called “trust.” Sometimes the right fix is a clearer approval process, a narrower permission, or a better explanation of what a verification badge means.

We can also reduce how much trust an action requires. Let an application read one file rather than an entire drive. Require another approval before releasing funds. Make a change reversible where possible.

More identity evidence isn’t automatically better, either. NIST’s identity-proofing guidance includes data minimization and usable options for people with different means and capabilities (Temoshok, Abruzzi, et al., 2025).

Evidence should address a relevant risk. Collecting more of it has costs.

Back to that file

You don’t need certainty about your colleague’s motives to make a sensible decision.

You need to know whether this disclosure is justified. That could mean checking the recipient’s authority, confirming the new address through an established route, or sharing less information. The FBI similarly recommends independent confirmation for consequential payment changes (FBI, n.d., 2024).

The useful question becomes:

What evidence would justify this action, given what I could lose?

That’s where this series starts. Stronger authentication gives us better evidence about account access. The next challenge is connecting that evidence to the decisions people actually face—without pretending we can certify another person’s future behavior.

What should a system show us before we decide to act?

References

Federal Bureau of Investigation. (2024, September 11). Business email compromise: The $55 billion scam (Alert No. I-091124-PSA). Internet Crime Complaint Center. https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240911

entry.summary: Why proving who we are isn't the same as knowing whom to trust.

entry.title: Michigan Is Rolling Out the Welcome Mat for Data Centers. Let’s Negotiate From the Front Porch.

link.title: Michigan Is Rolling Out the Welcome Mat for Data Centers. Let’s Negotiate From the Front Porch.

entry.content:
Data center construction amid Michigan’s rural landscape. Image source: Related Digital.

Originally written for and submitted to Bridge Michigan, this op-ed ultimately went unpublished. I’m sharing it here as part of my independent writing.

Michigan is rolling out the welcome mat for some of the largest data center projects in the country.

Not everyone is sure what to make of the new arrival.

The proposed Stargate campus in Saline Township and Google’s Project Cannoli in Van Buren Township represent billions of dollars in investment and signal Michigan’s ambition to compete in the rapidly growing artificial intelligence economy.

The scale is substantial. In its October 30, 2025 reporting, Michigan Advance described Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s announcement of the Saline Township project as the largest investment in Michigan history. The announced employment figures included 2,500 union construction jobs, 450 permanent jobs on site, and 1,500 additional jobs in the community. Those are projections, but they help explain why Michigan wants a place in this industry.

Supporters make a compelling case. In a recent Bridge Michigan guest commentary, OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane argued that building AI infrastructure presents a significant economic opportunity for the state.

Yet many residents are asking a different question:

What does Michigan get in return?

Across town halls, community meetings, and online discussions, concerns tend to sound remarkably similar. Residents see large developments consuming farmland, reshaping local landscapes, increasing demand on infrastructure, and placing new pressure on the electrical grid. Meanwhile, the promised benefits often arrive in the form of statistics about investment, tax revenue, and future economic growth.

Those benefits may be real. But they can also feel distant compared to the changes occurring directly outside someone’s front door.

The local concerns are not abstract either. Michigan Advance reported that the project moved forward after a legal settlement following the township board’s rejection of rezoning, amid opposition over traffic, noise, water, and energy. Welcoming investment does not make those questions disappear.

The answer is not to reject these projects.

The question is not whether Michigan should participate. The question is how Michigan can participate on the most advantageous terms possible.

AI Is Coming. Michigan Should Compete for It.

Whether artificial intelligence fulfills its most ambitious promises or falls short of them, one reality is already clear.

The race to build AI infrastructure is underway.

Technology companies, investors, utilities, and governments around the world are committing hundreds of billions of dollars to the data centers, power systems, and digital infrastructure required to support advanced computing. Analysts at McKinsey & Company estimate that AI-related data center investment could reach trillions of dollars globally over the coming years.

Michigan will not determine whether that transformation occurs.

The question is whether Michigan chooses to participate in it.

If the next generation of digital infrastructure is going to be built somewhere, there is a strong argument that some of it should be built here. The state has a skilled workforce, available land, strong utility partners, world-class universities, and a long history of supporting transformative industries.

Michigan should absolutely compete for these investments.

But competing for investment does not mean accepting whatever terms happen to be offered.

Communities Bring Value Too

Too often, discussions about economic development treat communities as passive beneficiaries.

They are not.

Communities contribute land, utility capacity, transportation infrastructure, public services, workforce development, and perhaps most importantly, the social license necessary for major projects to move forward.

Those contributions have value.

Michigan is not merely competing for investment. It is bringing assets to the negotiating table.

Michigan should approach these opportunities with confidence and a clear understanding of its own value.

The goal should not be to create barriers to investment. Nor should it be to demand symbolic concessions. The goal should be to identify opportunities where the interests of communities, utilities, residents, and developers align.

The most successful negotiations are not zero-sum. They create durable value for everyone involved.

In fact, communities across the country have already used Community Benefit Agreements to align major infrastructure and development projects with local priorities. These agreements demonstrate that economic development and community interests do not have to be competing objectives.

Saline Township offers a concrete example. Related Digital’s project page lists commitments of $8 million for area fire departments, $2 million for a community investment fund, and $4 million for a farmland preservation trust. It also projects at least $1.6 million in annual tax revenue through 2039 and $8 million for area schools.

Those commitments give the conversation a starting point. Communities should be able to understand when benefits arrive, who oversees them, and how promises become lasting results.

Thinking Bigger Than Tax Revenue

Public reporting suggests that projects such as Stargate and Project Cannoli could eventually require power measured in gigawatts. A recent WKAR analysis noted that the proposed developments could require electricity comparable to multiple large power plants. Likewise, the International Energy Agency has identified AI and data centers as a rapidly growing source of global electricity demand.

For Saline Township specifically, Michigan Advance reported DTE’s planned electrical load at 1.4 gigawatts. That makes the terms of power service a central community concern.

Related Digital says the project will finance new battery storage and that supplying its power will not affect existing DTE customers’ energy supply or rates. The developer also says closed-loop cooling will keep daily water use comparable to an office building. These are developer assurances that communities should be able to measure against actual performance.

Facilities operating at that scale are not simply commercial developments.

They become part of Michigan’s long-term infrastructure landscape.

That creates an opportunity to think beyond traditional economic development incentives.

Saline’s proposed battery investment makes that conversation especially relevant. Financing storage for a data center does not, by itself, establish what resilience benefits nearby residents will receive.

What if a project included community-scale battery storage that strengthened local grid resilience?

What if infrastructure investments helped keep hospitals, emergency services, and schools operating during major outages?

What if upgrades to the electrical system lowered costs or improved reliability for surrounding communities?

What if workforce development partnerships created pipelines into technical careers for Michigan students?

What if infrastructure improvements built to support data centers also strengthened the communities around them for decades to come?

These ideas are not merely theoretical. Community benefit agreements elsewhere have secured investments in workforce development, broadband access, education, and other community priorities through creative partnerships between developers and host communities. The Greenlining Institute has documented numerous examples of this approach in practice.

With enough creativity, the conversation becomes far more interesting than jobs versus opposition.

Instead, it becomes a discussion about how Michigan can use AI investment to build stronger communities.

The Michigan Way

Michigan has faced similar moments before.

The state did not become the center of the automotive industry simply because companies built factories here. Michigan invested in roads, utilities, manufacturing capacity, workforce development, and the infrastructure necessary to support long-term growth.

The result was not merely industrial success.

It was the creation of entire communities, industries, and generations of economic opportunity.

The AI economy presents a similar challenge.

The question is not whether AI comes to Michigan.

The question is what Michigan asks for when it arrives.

Michigan should welcome investment. It should compete aggressively for jobs, infrastructure, and technological leadership.

But it should also recognize the value it brings to the table and negotiate accordingly.

The strongest economic development strategies do more than attract capital.

They ensure that growth leaves the host community stronger than it found it.

Michigan has an opportunity not only to host the infrastructure powering the next generation of technology, but also to demonstrate how that growth can be shared.

Michigan is rolling out the welcome mat for data centers.

We should make sure we’re negotiating from the front porch, not watching through the window.
entry.summary: The piece argues that Michigan should actively compete for major AI and data center investments while ensuring host communities negotiate from a position of confidence and share in the long-term benefits of that growth. Rather than framing the discussion as a choice between development and opposition, the commentary explores how Michigan can participate in the emerging AI economy on terms that strengthen local infrastructure, resilience, and economic opportunity.
